nameStory: The "sleepy" in sleepy catchfly refers to its tiny, inconspicuous flowers that barely open, looking drowsy compared to their showier relatives. The "catchfly" name comes from the sticky bands found on the stems of many plants in this genus, which can trap small insects - though sleepy catchfly is less sticky than most of its cousins.
description: Sleepy catchfly is a slender annual wildflower that grows 6 inches to 3 feet tall with a delicate, wiry appearance. It produces tiny white or pinkish flowers that are so small they're easily overlooked - they barely open and seem to stay half-closed most of the time. The plant has a branching stem with narrow, opposite leaves and belongs to the pink family, though you'd never guess it from its modest blooms. It's one of those "blink and you'll miss it" wildflowers that rewards careful observation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale pink flowers less than 1/4 inch across that barely open, appearing sleepy or half-closed even in full bloom - unlike most flowers that open wide to show off

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, wiry annual with thin branching stems that feel delicate to the touch and sway easily in the breeze

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a smooth texture and no teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thin green stems that may have slightly sticky zones between the leaf joints, though less noticeably sticky than other catchflies

habitat: Look for sleepy catchfly in sandy or gravelly soils, disturbed areas, roadsides, and open fields throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained spots with full sun to partial shade and seems to prefer areas where the soil has been disturbed. You might find it growing alongside other weedy wildflowers in vacant lots, field edges, or along paths.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, and young plants develop their characteristic opposite leaves and branching structure.
seasonality.summer: Tiny flowers bloom from June through August, though they're so small and pale they're easily missed unless you look closely.
seasonality.fall: Plants set seed in small capsules and die back completely, leaving no winter trace since this is an annual species.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - seeds overwinter in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Despite being called a "catchfly," sleepy catchfly is actually one of the least sticky members of its genus - it seems to have traded its fly-catching superpowers for the ability to blend in so well that botanists have only recorded it 70 times in all of New England!
confusionNotes: The tiny flowers might be confused with small chickweeds, but chickweeds have alternate leaves while sleepy catchfly has opposite leaves. Remember: "Sleepy silene sits opposite" - the leaves are always in pairs across from each other on the stem.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this "catchfly" won't catch many flies! It's much less sticky than famous relatives like night-flowering catchfly, making it the wallflower of the catchfly world.
compareHints: Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open. While fire pink blazes with bright red blooms and white campion shows off pure white flowers, sleepy catchfly whispers with pale, half-closed petals. It's also less sticky than most other catchflies, lacking the pronounced gummy bands that give the group its name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
